title: localStorage
explain: localStorage is a browser-managed key-value store with one namespace per origin. It persists across reloads and browser restarts, is shared by all tabs of that origin, and is never sent to the server. It is synchronous, strings only and about 5 MB, so I use it for small preferences, not for secrets or big data.
model:
**One namespace per origin; origin = `scheme + host + port`.** The path does not matter.

```
https://app.example.com/settings   same store as   https://app.example.com:443/
http://app.example.com             different (scheme)
https://app.example.com:8443       different (port)
https://example.com                different (host)
```

What to remember:

- **Strings only** (`setItem(k, JSON.stringify(v))`), about 5 MB per origin.
- **Persistent:** no expiry; store your own timestamp or version.
- **Shared by all tabs** of the origin. Other tabs get a `storage` event; the tab that wrote does not.
- **Synchronous:** blocks the main thread; not available in Web Workers.
- **Never sent to the server** (unlike [cookies](#/sd/f/cookie)).
- **Readable by any script on the origin**, including XSS and third-party scripts: no tokens or secrets.

Good uses: UI preferences, draft text, cached non-sensitive data, a cross-tab signal. Outgrowing it: [IndexedDB](#/sd/f/indexeddb). Per-tab state: [sessionStorage](#/sd/f/session-storage).

details.q: Page loaded from https://app.example.com. Which of these share its localStorage: /settings/profile path, http:// scheme, :8443 port, the parent example.com, an explicit :443?
details.a: The path version and the explicit :443 do. Different scheme, different port and different host (even a parent domain) are different origins and different stores.

details.q: Tab A calls setItem('theme', 'dark'). What do the tabs see?
details.a: Tab B receives a `storage` event with the key, old and new value; tab A, which made the change, does not (it updates itself directly). That makes localStorage a convenient cross-tab signal.

details.q: A team stores the JWT access token in localStorage for their SPA. What is the downside?
details.a: Any script that runs on the page, including an XSS payload or a compromised third-party script, can read it. An `HttpOnly` cookie cannot be read by JavaScript, at the price of handling CSRF.

details.q: An editor writes a 2 MB JSON draft to localStorage on every keystroke and the UI stutters. Why, and what is better?
details.a: The API is synchronous, so each write blocks the main thread. Debounce the writes; for large or structured data use [IndexedDB](#/sd/f/indexeddb), which is asynchronous.

details.q: There is no expiry. How do you handle stale data?
details.a: Store a version and a timestamp with the value and discard what is old or from a previous schema on read. Also catch quota errors on write and the case where storage is unavailable (private modes, blocked storage).

details.q: Which four properties decide what you may put in localStorage?
details.a: Per origin and shared by tabs; persistent without expiry; synchronous, strings only and about 5 MB; readable by any script on the origin and never sent to the server. So: no secrets, nothing the server needs automatically, nothing large on a hot path.

details.q: Why not use it for per-tab state?
details.a: It is shared across tabs, so two tabs editing different drafts under the same key overwrite each other. Use [sessionStorage](#/sd/f/session-storage), or key by an id.

points: Key-value store, strings only, about 5 MB
One namespace per origin: scheme, host, port

prompts.q: What may you safely store in localStorage and what not?
points: Not: session tokens and secrets (XSS can read them)
Not: large data on hot paths (synchronous)
Not: anything the server needs automatically

prompts.q: Compare cookie, localStorage and IndexedDB for a web app.
points: Cookie: small, sent to the server on each request
Pick by size, visibility to the server and security
